ROLE: reporter
You write the final diagnosis of an incident from the evidence gathered. Every statement must be backed by evidence IDs taken from the evidence list; never invent an ID.

Root-cause categories (root_cause_category must be exactly one of these):
- bad_deployment: a new release introduced a defect (errors begin right after a deploy)
- db_connection_pool_exhaustion: every database connection in the pool is in use, so requests wait
- slow_query_missing_index: a database query became slow (for example a missing index)
- downstream_timeout: a dependency the service calls is slow or unresponsive
- memory_leak_oom: memory grows until the process is killed (OOM) and restarts
- disk_full: a volume is full so writes fail
- expired_tls_cert: a TLS certificate expired so handshakes fail
- misconfiguration: a wrong environment variable, setting or feature flag
- traffic_spike_rate_limit: request volume far above capacity, causing rate limiting or load shedding
- cache_stampede_outage: the cache is down or emptied so everything falls through to the database

Rules:
- claims: factual statements about what the evidence shows. Each cites one or more evidence IDs (log lines L-..., metrics M-..., runbook sections R-...) that actually support it.
- recommended_actions: concrete next steps for the on-call engineer, taken from the retrieved runbook sections. Each cites at least one runbook section ID (R-...).
- ruled_out: other hypotheses you considered and rejected, as short strings.
- confidence: low, medium or high.

Reply with only JSON in this shape:
{"incident_id": "INC-009", "root_cause_category": "disk_full", "root_cause_summary": "one or two sentences", "confidence": "high", "claims": [{"statement": "...", "evidence_ids": ["L-0123", "M-021"]}], "recommended_actions": [{"statement": "...", "evidence_ids": ["R-06-5"]}], "ruled_out": ["..."]}

Additional rules: choose the category that the evidence about the cause supports, not the one the symptoms suggest. downstream_timeout needs evidence that the dependency itself is slow or that calls to it timed out. Cite the evidence that identifies the cause (the telltale log line or the metric that changed), not only symptom lines.

Alert: search-service: HTTP error rate above 5% for 5 minutes (since 11:44 UTC)

Alert time: 2026-04-07T11:44:00Z
Data available from 2026-04-07T10:00:00Z to 2026-04-07T13:00:00Z

  Result: M-050: Change detected at 2026-04-07T11:40:00Z: mean 0.38 before, 25.86 after (229.2 baseline standard deviations).

Change detected at 2026-04-07T11:40:00Z: mean 0.38 before, 25.86 after (229.2 baseline standard deviations). Notable points: 2026-04-07T11:00:00Z = 0.16 (lowest); 2026-04-07T11:40:00Z = 25.9 (first point after the change); 2026-04-07T12:35:00Z = 26.09 (peak); 2026-04-07T12:40:00Z = 25.99 (last).

Step 4: log_search {"end": "2026-04-07T11:50:00Z", "limit": 30, "service": "search", "start": "2026-04-07T11:30:00Z"} (asked because: Search logs around the time the error rate jumped to identify deploy, config change, or specific error messages.)

Step 5: runbook_retrieve {"query": "bad deployment or bad release rollback mitigation"} (asked because: Retrieve mitigation steps for a bad deployment root cause.)
  Result: 3 runbook sections; best match R-01-3 (similarity 0.68).
  [R-01-3] Bad deployment or regression - How to confirm (similarity 0.68): Line the start of the trouble up against the release timeline. If it began just after a rollout and the previous version was healthy, suspect the release. Look at what the service wrote to its logs while the new version was starting and when the first failures arrived, and compare with an older instance if one is still running.
  [R-01-2] Bad deployment or regression - Symptoms (similarity 0.66): Things go wrong shortly after a rollout. Customers start seeing failures, dashboards turn red around the time the new version went out, and the problem does not fade by itself. The service may also restart a few times while the new version rolls through.
  [R-01-5] Bad deployment or regression - Mitigation (similarity 0.65): Go back to the previous release straight away by redeploying the last version known to be good. Do not spend time debugging on the live service first. Pause any further releases to this service until the cause is understood and a fix has been reviewed and tested.

Hypotheses from the investigation:
- bad_deployment: A new ranking model version was loaded into the search service at 11:38 UTC, and error rates jumped immediately after at 11:40 UTC without any preceding changes in CPU or memory utilization. (evidence: M-050, M-047, M-052, L-0289, L-0301)
- downstream_timeout: Logs indicate multiple 500 errors and upstream 503 responses when interacting with the cart service, suggesting a potential dependency issue or integration failure. (evidence: M-050, L-0305, L-0308, L-0327)
- misconfiguration: The timing of the incident right after a version change with stable resource usage could point to a bad configuration or feature flag bundled in the release. (evidence: M-050, M-047, M-052, L-0289)
